name: Palmyra
info: Palmyra is an ancient city in an oasis of central Syria, first named in documents of the early second millennium BCE, which grew rich on caravan trade, rebelled against Rome under Zenobia and was razed in 273 CE.

facts.founded: Settlement near the Efqa spring is dated to the Neolithic, with stone tools of about 7500 BCE; the city entered the written record around 2000 BCE, and a legend attributed its founding to Solomon.
facts.where: In an oasis of the Syrian Desert in central Syria, 215 km north-east of Damascus, between two mountain ranges and beside the wadi al-Qubur and the Efqa spring.
facts.known: Caravan trade between the Silk Road and the Mediterranean; the Temple of Bel; the Great Colonnade; tower tombs and funerary busts; King Odaenathus and Queen Zenobia; the Palmyrene Empire; its razing by Aurelian in 273
facts.today: The ancient site is a ruin beside the town of Tadmur, to which the villagers were moved in 1932, and it was declared a World Heritage Site in 1980.

t: Palmyra grew from a desert caravan station into a leading trading city in the first and second centuries CE, wealthy enough to build the Temple of Bel, the Great Colonnade and the tower tombs.
In the 260s King Odaenathus defeated the Sasanian emperor Shapur I, and his widow Zenobia ruled as regent for her son and rebelled against Rome until Aurelian defeated her and razed the city in 273.
The city shrank to a fortress, then a small village; Timur destroyed it in 1400, and in 1932 the villagers were moved to a new village so that the ancient site could be excavated.
dyk: At its height, around 270 in the reign of Zenobia, Palmyra had more than 200,000 residents, and by the beginning of the 20th century the village on the site had 6,000.
ev: Puzur-Ishtar the Tadmorean agrees to a contract at an Assyrian trading colony at Kultepe, the city's first appearance in the record
The Temple of Bel is dedicated
Hadrian visits, names the city Hadriane Palmyra and makes it a free city
Odaenathus defeats Shapur I near the Euphrates and becomes the ruler of a de facto allied kingdom
Aurelian razes the city after a rebellion
The Rashidun Caliphate takes the city under Khalid ibn al-Walid
Timur attacks and destroys the city, reducing it to a small village
The villagers are moved to the new village of Tadmur and the ancient site is opened to excavation

sections.origins:
Palmyra lies in an oasis in central Syria, 215 km north-east of Damascus, with the Syrian Desert to the south and east and two mountain ranges to the north and south-west. A small wadi, al-Qubur, crosses the area, and south of it is the spring of Efqa. Palmyra began as a small Neolithic settlement near the Efqa spring, where stone tools are dated to 7500 BCE. At Tell ez-Zor, near the spring, traces of settlement go back to the Prepottery Neolithic A period. A sounding in the tell beneath the Temple of Bel uncovered a Bronze Age mud-brick structure built around 2500 BCE.

The city entered the historical record around 2000 BCE, when Puzur-Ishtar the Tadmorean agreed to a contract at an Assyrian trading colony at Kultepe. Tablets from Mari of the 18th century BCE record the name as Ta-ad-mi-ir and mention the place as a stop for trade caravans and nomadic tribes, and Assyrian inscriptions of the 11th century BCE give it as Ta-ad-mar. The Hebrew Bible records a desert city called Tadmor, built or fortified by Solomon, and Josephus attributed the founding of Palmyra to him. That association is a conflation of Tadmor with a city Solomon built in Judea, and Palmyra was a small settlement in the 10th century BCE. The origin of the name is unclear; the standard interpretation connects it to the Semitic word for date palm, tamar.
sections.growth:
Under the Seleucids, between 312 and 64 BCE, Palmyra became a prosperous settlement. In the middle of the Hellenistic era it began to expand beyond the northern bank of the wadi, and by the late 2nd century BCE the tower tombs of the Valley of Tombs and the first city temples were being built. During the first century CE it developed from a minor desert caravan station into a leading trading centre, with Palmyrene merchants establishing colonies in surrounding trade centres. The city's first walled fortifications were built in that century, and the Temple of Bel was dedicated in 32 CE.

Palmyrene trade reached its peak in the second century, helped by a trade route that the Palmyrenes built and protected with garrisons, and by the Roman conquest of Petra in 106, which moved control of the southern trade routes from the Nabataeans to Palmyra. Hadrian visited in 129, named the city Hadriane Palmyra and made it a free city. The projects of this period included the theatre, the colonnade and the Temple of Nabu. At its height, around 270 in the reign of Zenobia, Palmyra had more than 200,000 residents. Its economy rested on agriculture, pastoralism, taxation and above all the caravan trade. Silk, exported from East to West, was the main income-earning good, and the Harbaqa Dam, built in the late first century CE, can collect 140,000 cubic metres of water.
sections.rulers:
Palmyra changed hands between several empires. It owed allegiance to the Seleucid king until 64 BCE, when Rome conquered the Seleucid kingdom and Pompey established the province of Syria. Palmyra was left independent, trading with Rome and Parthia but belonging to neither. Mark Antony sent a force against it in 41 BCE, and it became part of the Roman Empire around 14 CE, early in the reign of Tiberius, keeping much of its internal autonomy. In the 190s it was assigned to the new province of Phoenice, and Caracalla made it a colonia between 213 and 216.

Odaenathus appears as lord of Palmyra in an inscription of 252. After Shapur I defeated and captured the emperor Valerian in 260, Odaenathus won a victory over the Persians near the Euphrates and received from Gallienus the title Imperator Totius Orientis. Palmyra became in practice an allied kingdom. He was assassinated in 267 and succeeded by his ten-year-old son Vaballathus, with the boy's mother Zenobia as de facto ruler. From 270 she conquered Roman Arabia and Egypt, then invaded Anatolia and reached Ankara. Aurelian defeated her at Immae and Emesa and besieged Palmyra; Zenobia was captured and the city capitulated. After 273 Rome ruled it directly.

The Rashidun Caliphate took the city in 634, and it later belonged to the Umayyad and Abbasid caliphates. In the 12th century the Burids, the Zengids and then the Ayyubids held it, and under the Mamluks the Al Fadl clan governed it. It came under Ottoman rule in the 16th century and, with Syria, under the French Mandate after 1920.
sections.life:
Palmyra's people combined elements of Amorites, Arameans and Arabs. The earliest known inhabitants were Amorites, Arameans were recorded by the end of the second millennium BCE, and Arabs arrived in the late first millennium BCE and were assimilated. The city also had a Jewish community, and Greeks were few and restricted in their settlement. The Palmyrenes spoke Palmyrene Aramaic and used Greek for commercial and diplomatic purposes. The last Palmyrene inscription dates to 279/280, and after the Arab conquest Greek was replaced by Arabic.

Thirty clans are documented, and by the time of Nero the city had four tribes, each living in a quarter bearing its name. A council of about six hundred members of the local elite supervised public works, approved expenditure, collected taxes and appointed two archons each year. Women commissioned inscriptions, buildings and tombs, and in some cases held administrative offices. The chief deity was Bol, later called Bel, with over sixty ancestral gods of the clans beside him. Christianity replaced this worship, and a bishop was reported in the city by 325.

The Palmyrenes buried their dead in family mausoleums, with a relief of the person interred on the wall as a headstone, and many tombs held mummies embalmed in a way similar to that of ancient Egypt. The Great Colonnade, 1.1 km long, was the main street, and the large agora resembled an eastern caravanserai more than a Greek public square.
sections.crises:
The greatest disaster of the ancient city came in 273. Aurelian had spared Palmyra and left a garrison of 600 archers, but the city rebelled under Septimius Apsaios and declared Antiochus, a relative of Zenobia, Augustus. Aurelian marched against it, razed it, and took its most valuable monuments to decorate his Temple of Sol. Buildings were smashed, residents massacred and the Temple of Bel pillaged. Palmyra was significantly reduced and largely disappeared from the historical record. Diocletian later restored it at a reduced size, with a wall enclosing about 80 hectares, much smaller than the city before 273.

Palmyra's loyalty to the Umayyads brought an aggressive military response from the Abbasids, and the city diminished in size, losing its merchant class. In 745 Marwan II ordered its walls demolished. Earthquakes devastated it in 1068 and 1089. In 1400 Timur attacked Palmyra; according to Sharaf ad-Din Ali Yazdi, his men took 200,000 sheep, and the city was reduced to a settlement on the desert border whose inhabitants herded animals and cultivated small plots.

During the Syrian civil war the Islamic State captured Palmyra in May 2015 and destroyed large parts of the ancient city, among them the Temple of Bel and the Temple of Baalshamin. It held the city again from December 2016 to March 2017.
sections.legacy:
Palmyra's first scholarly description appeared in 1695, and in 1751 an expedition led by Robert Wood and James Dawkins studied its architecture. Louis-François Cassas surveyed its monuments in 1785. Its funerary busts reached Western museums in large numbers in the 19th century and became evidence in an art-historical debate about Eastern influence on Roman art. The Palmyra Tariff, a stone slab of 137 CE inscribed in Greek and Palmyrene with the city's tax law, was discovered in the Tariff Court in 1882 and has been described as one of the most important single items of evidence for the economic life of any part of the Roman Empire.

Henri Seyrig began large-scale excavation in 1929, starting with the Temple of Bel, and persuaded the villagers, who lived within the ruins, to move to a new French-built village next to the site. The move was completed in 1932, and the villagers settled in Tadmur. In 1980 the historic site, including the necropolis outside the walls, was declared a World Heritage Site by UNESCO. Most of Palmyra remains unexplored, especially the residential quarters in the north and south.

Palmyra today is an ancient site in central Syria beside the town of Tadmur. The Valley of Tombs west of the walls, a necropolis one kilometre long, holds more than 50 monuments, mostly tower tombs.

summary: Palmyra is an ancient city in a Syrian oasis that grew wealthy from caravan trade. Under Odaenathus and Zenobia it ruled much of the Roman East until Aurelian razed it in 273. Timur destroyed it again in 1400, and it is now a ruin beside Tadmur.
references: Warwick Ball, Rome in the East: The Transformation of an Empire (Routledge, 2002)
Trevor Bryce, Ancient Syria: A Three Thousand Year History (Oxford University Press, 2014)
Kevin Butcher, Roman Syria and the Near East (The British Museum Press, 2003)
Malcolm Andrew Richard Colledge, The Art of Palmyra (Thames & Hudson, 1976)
notes: START: the article gives no founding date. Settlement near Efqa is Neolithic (stone tools 7500 BCE; a Bronze Age structure c. 2500 BCE); I used c. 2000 BCE, when the city enters the record (Puzur-Ishtar at Kultepe), with circa true. No 'History of Palmyra' article was available; the city article alone was used.
Population: 'more than 200,000' at its height around 270 is the article's figure (undated more closely); the village of 6,000 is the beginning of the 20th century.

Aurelian: the article says he levelled the city in 273 after a rebellion, and also that Zenobia's capture came before the city capitulated; it dates the Battles of Immae and Emesa only by 'the following year' after 271, so I gave no year for them. In the lead the city is 'levelled', in the History 'razing it to the ground'; both used as given. The Temple of Bel was repaired by Aurelian afterwards, which I left out.

Diocletian: the lead says Diocletian restored the city at reduced size; the History says the Camp of Diocletian was built shortly before 303 and that Aurelian erected the wall (enclosing about 80 hectares). I wrote 'Diocletian later restored it' and attributed the 80-hectare wall to the rampart without naming the builder.

Temple of Bel: the article says it was dedicated in 32 AD in the layout section's list and 'completed and dedicated in 32 AD' in History; also 139 rebuilding by Male' Agrippa, left out. Dedication 32 used.
The Harbaqa Dam 'can collect' 140,000 cubic metres: article's present-tense figure, kept.

2015 destruction told as a bare dated fact as instructed: IS captured Palmyra May 2015, destroyed large parts, held it again Dec 2016 to Mar 2017. The article names the Temple of Bel and the Temple of Baalshamin as destroyed in 2015 (the Monumental Arch too, left out). The deaths of Khaled al-Asaad and executions in the theatre, the 2017 recapture, the 2024 events and restoration projects were left out as present-day matters.

Ottoman: article says Palmyra was not incorporated before the conquest of Iraq in 1534-1535 although Syria fell in 1516; I wrote only 'in the 16th century'. French Mandate: Syria became part of it after the Battle of Maysalun, 24 July 1920; I wrote 'after 1920'.
Umayyad prosperity and the souq, the Banu Kalb, Mamluk Al Fadl princes, the Burid citadel of 1132 and the Ayyubid castle omitted for space except as named.
Language: the article offers several theories for the disappearance of Palmyrene; I gave only the dated last inscription (279/280) and the later replacement of Greek by Arabic.
Name etymology: the article discusses Hurrian, Syriac and Greek-origin theories; only the standard date-palm interpretation is given.
Sources of doubt on ethnicity (Aramean or Arab) left out except the combined description; the article says it is debated.

In 'rulers' I wrote that the Seleucids held Palmyra until 64 BCE, as the article says Palmyra was under them between 312 and 64 BCE; the article does not say it was ruled by earlier Persians or Alexander's successors.
